n0001.title: Spider silk
n0001.gist: Spider silk's toughness and versatility across natural uses now drive efforts to replicate it synthetically for new applications.
n0001.question: Spider silk — why is it valued enough to drive both natural uses and synthetic replication? (an overview)

n0002.title: What spider silk is
n0002.gist: Spiders spin silk from specialized glands to build webs, trap and restrain prey, protect eggs, travel through air, and signal mates.
n0002.question: Spider silk — what roles does it play in a spider's life? (several functions)

n0003.title: Overview of spider silk
n0003.gist: Spiders spin protein-based silk from internal glands to build webs and other structures that trap prey, restrain it, relay touch signals, or shelter their offspring.

n0009.title: Silk, food, and courtship
n0009.gist: Beyond web-building, spiders sometimes eat their own silk for nutrition, and silk threads carry courtship signals and pheromones between males and females during mating.

n0012.title: Properties
n0012.gist: Spider silk's layered protein structure gives it an unusual mix of strength, stretchiness, and toughness that varies by type and conditions, plus strong adhesive properties.
n0012.question: Properties — why does spider silk outperform comparable materials in toughness and adhesion? (several measured properties)

n0013.title: Structural properties
n0013.gist: Spider silk's proteins form repeating glycine- and alanine-rich blocks that create hard crystalline regions within a stretchy amorphous matrix, and added chemicals protect the fiber from microbes and decay.

n0021.title: Mechanical
n0021.gist: Spider silk combines high tensile strength with great stretchiness, giving it exceptional toughness that varies by species and silk type and depends on humidity, temperature, and molecular alignment.

n0048.title: Adhesive
n0048.gist: A two-part secretion forms durable 'attachment discs' that bond instantly, work indefinitely, biodegrade naturally, and whose stickiness is controlled by the spider's spinnerets.

n0051.title: Uses and silk types
n0051.gist: Spiders produce several structurally distinct silks, each made by its own gland and suited to a specific use, from prey capture to reproduction and travel.
n0051.question: Uses and silk types — how do different silk types match different spider needs? (several silk types)

n0052.title: Uses
n0052.gist: A single spider can produce up to seven silk types for distinct purposes—capturing and immobilizing prey, reproduction, dispersal, nest-building, safety lines, and pheromone trails—unlike most silk-producing insects.

n0056.title: Silk type categories
n0056.gist: Different glands produce structurally distinct silks—dragline, scaffolding, capture-spiral, egg-sac, wrapping, sticky, and bonding silks—each matched to a specific structural or adhesive role in the web.

n0063.title: Silk type functions
n0063.gist: Each silk type carries a specialized function, from the strong and tough dragline and wrapping silks to the stretchy capture-spiral and stiff egg-sac silk.

n0067.title: Synthesis and fibre spinning
n0067.gist: Spider silk forms as liquid protein is pulled through a tapering duct inside specialized glands, where chemical and mechanical changes convert it into solid fiber.
n0067.question: Synthesis and fibre spinning — how does a spider turn liquid protein into solid silk thread? (the gland process)

n0068.title: Spinning process
n0068.gist: Unlike continuously grown materials, silk is pulled on demand from a liquid precursor stored in glands, a process resembling pultrusion rather than true spinning or extrusion.

n0073.title: Silk gland anatomy
n0073.gist: Silk forms as proteins self-assemble into micelles, align under shear while passing through a tapering duct, and solidify as pH drops and water is removed before exiting the spigot.

n0085.title: Araneus gland example
n0085.gist: In the garden cross spider, several hundred glands of different types—pyriform, ampullate, aciniform, tubuliform, aggregate, and coronate—each produce silk for a distinct purpose, illustrating the system's complexity.

n0094.title: Artificial synthesis
n0094.gist: Reproducing spider silk artificially requires both a suitable protein feedstock and a device mimicking the spider's spinning duct, and various organisms and methods have been tried with partial success.
n0094.question: Artificial synthesis — why has replicating natural spider silk proven so difficult? (several approaches)

n0095.title: Feedstock
n0095.gist: Replicating spider silk requires extracting its complex, long protein from organisms such as silkworms, bacteria, goats, or plants, though produced fibers rarely match natural silk's strength.

n0102.title: Geometry
n0102.gist: Because the silk's molecules are relatively simple, artificial fiber-spinning methods—syringes, superhydrophobic surfaces, sheets, microfluidics, and electrospinning—must recreate the spider's complex duct geometry to form effective fibers.

n0117.title: Synthetic silk applications
n0117.gist: Spider silk proteins can be shaped into capsules, membranes, and fibers for medical and industrial use, and companies have engineered bacteria, yeast, silkworms, goats, and custom devices to manufacture synthetic versions.

n0131.title: Research
n0131.gist: A handful of landmark papers since the 1960s established spider silk's chemistry, structure, mechanics, and spinning process, shaping how it is understood today.
n0131.question: Research — which studies built the modern understanding of spider silk? (a table of key papers)

n0134.title: Human uses
n0134.gist: Humans have tried to harvest and apply spider silk since the 1700s, using it in textiles, medicine, optics, and scientific instruments despite persistent production difficulties.
n0134.question: Human uses — how have people tried to put spider silk to practical use? (several applications)

n0135.title: Early attempts and applications
n0135.gist: Early 18th-century efforts to weave spider silk failed commercially, and even modern mass production remains so difficult that the largest cloth piece took eighty-two workers four years to make.

n0140.title: Medicine
n0140.gist: Spider silk has traditionally been used to dress wounds for its antiseptic, clotting-aiding properties, and modern research has explored it for regenerating mammalian nerve tissue.

n0143.title: Science and technology
n0143.gist: Spider silk's fineness and elasticity make it useful for optical crosshairs, diffraction experiments, biolenses, and suspending fusion targets without introducing unwanted x-ray-emitting elements.
